Allen Oliver   Graduate of the Kentucky Psychoanalytic Institute and a NAAP certified psychoanalyst in private practice in Louisville, KY. Licensed as a Marriage and Family Therapist, he is both a Clinical Member and an Approved Supervisor of the American Association for Marriage and Family Therapy. Oliver is also a Diplomate in the American Psychotherapy Association and a Fellow of the American Association of Pastoral Counselors. A forty-year-old woman has an unresolved masculinity complex leaving her enraged and giving rise to her desire to reap vengeance on her mother and her husband. This has led to the schizophrenic response, as her rage overwhelms even the narcissistic defense. In the course of treatment, both she and her analyst struggle to remain grounded in reality while sublimating her rage into her creative work as an artist.

The author shares with us the experiences that surrounded the death of his mother-in-law, the way in which the family responded to her death, and the effect it had, most particularly, on his wife as she wrestled with what seemed to be her mother's desire to “get even” just before dying. Meadow Institute in Dummerston, VT. He has lectured and written on diverse subjects including fantasy, creativity, marriage, impulsivity, violence, and the psychology of men.

As a feeling of connection and a feeling of esteem, or worth, are the two most basic psychological needs, their negation—abandonment and humiliation, respectively—are the two most profound psychological injuries. “Revenge is sweet” in response to these injuries. “Getting even” is an attempt to restore esteem and/or connection (even if only in death). Personal, historical and clinical anecdotes illustrate these points, and demonstrate how the revenge motive may be defused, diverted into fantasy, or directed into constructive action.

Elizabeth Dorsey

Elizabeth Dorsey

Elizabeth Dorsey  

Eminent Harvard Medical School professor J. Alan Hobson and writer Jonathan Leonard have teamed up to write an eloquent wakeup call for psychiatry in the United States today. Hobson, who directs the Laboratory of Neurophysiology at the Massachusetts Mental Health Center, and Leonard launch a scathing evaluation of the failures of a field and a society to care for the approximately three out of every one hundred adults in this country who suffer from severe mental illness.

Using case vignettes, largely from Hobson's experience and public knowledge, they lay the foundation for their recommendations, first, by defining the problems. Their brief history of psychiatry holds no shortage of criticism for either the medicalization of care or what they term “humanist” approaches of psychoanalysis and other psychologies. “Today's psychiatry,” they write, “is about where communicable disease medicine was [in World War I]. Until recently we could do little to combat severe disorders of the mind. We had no idea what caused them; our asylums were little more than holding tanks; and Freudian progress was disappointing” (pp. 16-17).

Psychoanalysis offered hope to physicians charged with the huge numbers of severely ill patients housed in massive institutions, and, in the 1920s, the American medical community embraced Freud's discipline and claimed it exclusively. Young doctors sought psychiatric training and the opportunity for a personal analysis and time talking with psychotic patients. Analysts chaired departments in all the most prestigious medical schools.

This paper explores the internal conflicts that may derail efforts to undertake or complete a dissertation. In the review of literature on this subject and in several illuminating case studies, the author focuses on four indicators: fantasy of the meaning and significance of doctoral dissertation; evidence of drive fusion or defusion; sexual identity and object choice difficulties; and potential for drive satisfaction. As the language of the unconscious, humor provides an important means to “get even” with the patient, i.e., to be at the same level with the patient. The author discusses Freud's ambivalence to the use of humor as well as his economic theory of releasing impulses and relaxing defenses. Freud's later characterization of the superego as a benevolent, rather than harsh, agent provides clinical cues for the use of humor that relate to Spotnitz's clinical approach. Spotnitz's varied joining and mirroring techniques are seen as being with the patient on many levels in a humorous manner that illustrate how unconscious forces can be constructively integrated and released.

Frances Bigda-Peyton   Faculty of the Institute for the Study of Violence and serves as field work coordinator for that program. She frequently lectures on innovative approaches to couples therapy. She is in private practice in Brookline, MA.

Overconsumption of resources has been identified as a major cause of current environmental problems. Psychoanalysts have begun shedding light on the intrapsychic and group dynamics underlying this phenomenon. Their contributions are herein reviewed. Drive theory adds an understanding of the death instinct. Humans have inherent tendencies to destroy and use up. Harmful overconsumption occurs when psychic structures dominated by destructive instincts succeed in overpowering life-sustaining impulses. Overconsumption also functions as a defense against the awareness of death wishes. Narcissistic fixations keep individuals and groups from maturing to the point of recognizing that they must give to the environment in order to be provided for in a sustainable way.

This recent edition of the collected papers of Louis Ormont offers a treasure trove of guidelines and strategies for use in mining the inherent power of the group as an agent of personal growth and maturation. Covering a forty-year period from the 1950s to the present this collection narrates the evolution of the author's intense and ceaseless study of the group processes as they unfolded in thousands of group sessions conducted by him.

The earliest papers address the preparation of patients for group therapy and the importance of the therapeutic contract in providing a structure in which the resistances of individuals and groups to telling the meaningful story of their lives can be identified and studied. Five seminal papers examine the cornerstone concept of resistance: the treatment of preoedipal resistance in the group setting, resistances to immediacy and intimacy, the management of aggression as resistance, and resistances conjoint treatment. A paper on the use of the objective countertransference written in 1970, long before the broad recognition of the value of using the induced feelings, illustrates the author's unusual prescience. Other papers carefully address the author's research on the development of emotional insulation in groups, facilitating the observing ego, and one of the author's major concepts, bridging. In addition, there is a valuable section on the training of group therapists.

An important contribution of modern psychoanalysis to the field of mental health treatment is its commitment to work with extremely regressed patients. To work with such a patient population depends heavily on therapists' understanding of their own reactions as well as of patients' dynamics. Training to achieve these goals is an essential aspect of becoming a professional in this field.

This paper examines the mental health fieldwork experience as described by students and faculty in two modern psychoanalytic training centers and proposes seven criteria by which the student therapist's growth in understanding the narcissistic patient can be measured. They are: the student's observation of the contact function; the student's interventions; the student's defenses and reactions to those defenses; the student's descriptions of the patient's symbolic and unconscious verbal and nonverbal communications; the student's reactions to the patient and an understanding of those reactions; the student's reactions to supervision;

This case study examines a three-year period in the psychoanalytic treatment of a man who was both a sexual offender and a sun'ivor of childhood sexual abuse. Single-Case-Study Methodology and the Contact Function

Mary Shepherd MA

Mary Shepherd

36 Hawthorn Street
Cambridge, MA 02138
maryshepherd@comcast.net

Mary Shepherd   Training and supervising analyst and an associate professor at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis where she is also the public information officer. She has written on modern psychoanalytic history and anaclitic countertransference considerations. Her current research interest involves the attempt to integrate aspects of psychoanalytic meta-theory with the recent discoveries of neuroscience.

Modern analysts have spent over three decades refining a methodology for single-case-study research that is both appropriate for psychoanalysis and acceptable to the canons of scientific inquiry. This paper suggests that the modern psychoanalytic concept of the contact function is an important contribution to this work. The contact function is a window on the unconscious functioning of the patient in the transference and can therefore be used to ensure that the universe of observation is non-reactive. It also functions as an indicator of closeness or distance to the analyst and so can provide a check on the findings.

Revenge has many faces: it can be a constructive way of directing rage onto another rather than at the self; it is an unavoidable outcome of the parent-child relationship; in many cultures, its principles are embedded in the law; and, in its starkest form, it is a desire to obliterate the offender. The author examines these various perspectives on revenge and shares the story of a woman, much like herself, who in a moment of rage and passion murdered her mother. In closing she discusses solutions to help us deal with the power of our destructive drive.

Rodrigo Barahona MA

Rodrigo Barahona

321 Summit Avenue #5

Rodrigo Barahona   Private practice in Brookline, MA. He is also a psychotherapist with the outpatient unit at Arbour Hospital and the substance abuse unit of the Boston Public Health Commission. He is an advanced psychoanalytic candidate at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis Certificate Program and is finalizing his doctorate studies at the Cyril Z. Meadow Institute of Psychoanalysis in Vermont.

Is modern psychoanalysis only a theory of technique? In a critique and defense of modern psychoanalysis, the author describes what he views as the primary epistemological difficulties in modern psychoanalytic theory, vis-a-vis the greater psychoanalytic community, that may be contributing to an “existential crisis” in its theory and theorists. Drawing from the work of other psychoanalytic traditions, the author argues that far from being just a theory of technique and, therefore, lacking as far as mind theory, modern psychoanalysis is embedded in traditional and contemporary theory, theoretical introjects of a sort, whether this is formally recognized or not. For example, the author describes how, in his view, Spotnitz and Meadow's conception of the development and workings of the early infantile psyche and of pathology can be alternatively understood as a theory of internal object relations, indeed, that a theory of

271

internal object relations is implicit in their work. From this perspective, the author attempts to clarify what in modern analytic literature could be described as the “killing off” or the “death” of the object in narcissism and, more specifically, schizophrenia and concludes that in both of these states the object is never truly dead.

Steven Poser   Coordinator of the research committee and training analyst at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. An exhibiting painter, he received the 1997 NAAP Gradiva award for visual art, He is in private practice in New York City and Salt Point, NY.

The case study is widely used in psychoanalysis for presenting and illustrating clinical theory. It is also the standard means by which analysts-in-training demonstrate their ability both to manage cases and to convey their grasp of the case material. Most training institutes use the formal presentation of a case as a requirement for graduation. The Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, New York, currently requires a single-case study as a final piece for the completion of certificate training (Meadow & Bernstein, 1999). In this paper we argue that the main purpose of the training case study is to illustrate theory systematically in clinical material and that treating the case study as an illustration addresses the main controversies over the legitimacy of the case study as a research method and, in particular, suits the needs of clinical training. In the light of this we set out a structure for the case study, giving its components and sequence and a rationale for this structure.

Faye Newsome   Private practice in New York City and Boston. She is on the faculties of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis where she is a training and control analyst, and a supervisor. She is also the Liaison Officer for the proposed master's degree to be offered by BGSP at CMPS. This year she has led monthly case seminars for students, faculty, and other clinicians at CMPS. She is also co-director of the BGSP Therapy Center. Her writings and workshop presentations focus on clinical issues which has led to her interest in the psychoanalytic concept of envy, the subject of a doctoral dissertation that she is developing.

The psychoanalytic literature often traces the roots of negative therapeutic reactions to an inability to tolerate the experience of envy. Allowing conscious recognition of the envy would require an ability to be tolerant of one's dependence on the goodness of an object. The article explores the connections between envy, narcissism, negative therapeutic reactions, revenge, and protection of the object field of the mind.

Lucy Holmes PHD

Lucy Holmes

52 East 78th St. #2A

Lucy Holmes   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and Ridgewood, NJ. Formerly the Executive Director of the Center for Group Studies, she currently serves on its faculty and board. She is also President of the Society of Modern Psychoanalysts. Author of many articles on women and women in group, her “The Object Within: Childbirth as a Developmental Milestone” was awarded the Gradiva Award as best article of 2002, by the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis.

Three of the most popular ways that women seek revenge are by suffering, by seduction, and by repeating in unconscious identification. The author presents clinical examples of aggressive suffering by two women, one very rich and one very poor, as well as the example of a beautiful dancer who got even by seducing the analyst and breaking her heart. Finally, the author describes a particularly malevolent case of revenge carried out in a women's group using repetition and unconscious identification with a cruel father. All three of these methods have major drawbacks. The author concludes with a brief description of some more constructive ways of getting even.
